---
title: "Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium"
description: "Genotype frequencies after one generation of random mating."
---

## The idea

In a large, randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration, allele and genotype frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. If allele *A*~1~ has frequency *p* and *A*~2~ has frequency *q* = 1 − *p*, then after one generation of random mating the genotype frequencies are

$$
A_1A_1 : A_1A_2 : A_2A_2 \;=\; p^2 : 2pq : q^2 .
$$

Heterozygotes are most common when *p* = 0.5, where 2*pq* = 0.5. When an allele is rare, almost all copies of it are carried in heterozygotes, which is why selection against a rare recessive is so slow.

*Source: Falconer & Mackay, chapter 1.*

## Widget

Set the allele frequency, then draw a finite sample of individuals to see how much observed genotype counts scatter around the Hardy–Weinberg expectation.

```{ojs}
viewof p = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "Frequency of A₁ (p)"})
viewof n = Inputs.range([10, 1000], {value: 100, step: 10, label: "Sample size (individuals)"})
viewof seed = Inputs.button("Draw a new sample", {value: 1, reduce: v => v + 1})
```

```{ojs}
expected = [
  {genotype: "A₁A₁", freq: p * p},
  {genotype: "A₁A₂", freq: 2 * p * (1 - p)},
  {genotype: "A₂A₂", freq: (1 - p) * (1 - p)}
]

sample = {
  const rng = d3.randomLcg(seed * 7919 + Math.round(p * 1000) + n);
  const counts = {"A₁A₁": 0, "A₁A₂": 0, "A₂A₂": 0};
  for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const a = rng() < p, b = rng() < p;
    counts[a && b ? "A₁A₁" : a || b ? "A₁A₂" : "A₂A₂"]++;
  }
  return Object.entries(counts).map(([genotype, c]) => ({genotype, freq: c / n, count: c}));
}

chiSq = d3.sum(sample, (d, i) => {
  const e = expected[i].freq * n;
  return e > 0 ? (d.count - e) ** 2 / e : 0;
})
```

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  height: 280,
  marginLeft: 50,
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "Frequency", grid: true},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Expected (HWE)", "Observed sample"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barY(
      [...expected.map(d => ({...d, kind: "Expected (HWE)"})),
       ...sample.map(d => ({...d, kind: "Observed sample"}))],
      {x: "kind", fx: "genotype", y: "freq", fill: "kind", tip: true}
    ),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ],
  fx: {label: null},
  x: {axis: null}
})
```

```{ojs}
md`Observed counts: **${sample.map(d => `${d.genotype} = ${d.count}`).join(", ")}**.
χ² against HWE expectation = **${chiSq.toFixed(2)}** (1 df; values above 3.84 would be called a significant departure at α = 0.05, which happens about 5% of the time by chance alone).`
```

### Genotype frequencies across all values of *p*

```{ojs}
curve = d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.01).flatMap(x => [
  {p: x, freq: x * x, genotype: "A₁A₁"},
  {p: x, freq: 2 * x * (1 - x), genotype: "A₁A₂"},
  {p: x, freq: (1 - x) ** 2, genotype: "A₂A₂"}
])

Plot.plot({
  height: 300,
  marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Frequency of A₁ (p)"},
  y: {label: "Genotype frequency", domain: [0, 1], grid: true},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(curve, {x: "p", y: "freq", stroke: "genotype", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.ruleX([p], {strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
    Plot.dot(expected, {x: () => p, y: "freq", fill: "genotype", r: 5, tip: true})
  ]
})
```

## Things to try

- Set *p* = 0.05. Only 0.25% of individuals are *A*~1~*A*~1~, but 9.5% carry *A*~1~ as heterozygotes, so nearly every copy of a rare allele is hidden in a heterozygote.
- Use a small sample (*n* = 20) and redraw several times. Departures that look large are often just sampling noise.
